authoredPrompt: This figure has two panels, (a) and (b), each drawing a convex polygon over labeled points in the plane. In (a) a light gray polygon labeled Q_j fills the right portion; its boundary runs from p_0 at the bottom left up to p_j at the top, right through p_k and two unlabeled black dots, down the right side to p_2, and back along the bottom through p_1 to p_0. A darker gray triangle is attached along the left, with corners p_0, p_j, and a further point p_i lying outside to the left, so that the two shaded regions together form a larger polygon whose boundary now passes through p_i. In (b) the hull boundary is a thick gray chain from p_0 rightward to p_1, up the right side, and back across the top through p_j; at the left a thin-outlined light gray triangle has corners p_i, p_r just to its right, and p_0 at the bottom, and a point p_t sits inside that triangle. Dashed segments join p_i and p_r to p_t, and a small arc marks the angle at p_t. Placing the panels side by side contrasts a point that enlarges the hull with a point enclosed by three others and therefore incapable of being a hull vertex. The pair underpins the correctness argument for Graham's scan, where each newly considered point either joins the stack or forces an earlier point off it.
authoredInteractions:
- Toggle between the left-turn case in panel (a) and the nonleft-turn case in panel (b): the candidate point either expands the shaded hull or is shown inside the triangle, making clear how turn direction determines hull membership.
- Button for stepping through the Graham-scan stack update: each press tests the next labeled point, draws the relevant angle, and either pushes the point or removes the interior point, making clear why nonleft turns cannot remain on the convex hull.
- Click for p_i, p_j, p_r, or p_t: the selected point and its supporting triangle or hull edge highlight, making clear which surrounding points prove that it belongs on or inside the hull.
authoredContext: Theorem 33.1 (Correctness of Graham’s scan) If GRAHAM-SCAN executes on a set Q of points, where jQj _x0015_ 3, then at termination, the stack S consists of, from bottom to top, exactly the vertices of CH.Q/ in counterclockwise order. Proof After line 2, we have the sequence of points hp1; p2; : : : ; pmi. Let us define, for i D 2; 3; : : : ; m, the subset of points Qi D fp0; p1; : : : ; pi g. The points in Q Qm are those that were removed because they had the same polar angle relative to p0 as some point in Qm; these points are not in CH.Q/, and so CH.Qm/ D CH.Q/. Thus, it suffices to show that when GRAHAM-SCAN terminates, the stack S consists of the vertices of CH.Qm/ in counterclockwise order, when listed from bottom to top. Note that just as p0, p1, and pm are vertices of CH.Q/, the points p0, p1, and pi are all vertices of CH.Qi/. The proof uses the following loop invariant: At the start of each iteration of the for loop of lines 9–12, stack S consists of, from bottom to top, exactly the vertices of CH.Qi1/ in counterclockwise order

evaluation.notes: The figure faithfully reproduces both panels of the Graham scan turn-test illustration with correct topology, fills, dashed lines, and angle arc; the step-through scan interaction is pedagogically excellent and conceptually accurate, but labels are uncomfortably small at inline rendering size and panel (a) is missing one hull vertex compared to the source.
